text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARYCOMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 1 The state of commodity markets The outlook for commodity markets has become increasingly complex amid potentially reinforcing shocks related to multiple conflict fronts and an unusually powerful El Niño. Crude oil exports from the Gulf region have recently been close to preconflict volumes, aided by pipeline flows and workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers beyond the Strait of Hormuz. Nonetheless, flows of refined oil products from the region have remained depressed amid damage to refineries, at less than half of preconflict levels in September. Meanwhile attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline and threats to shipping in the Red Sea highlight the potential vulnerability of alternative export routes for crude oil that helped to attenuate disruptions this year.

After dipping in August, global oil production picked up in September but still fell short of global consumption (figure 1.A). Against this backdrop, Brent crude prices reached about $110 per barrel ($/bbl) in mid-October. Since March, the oil market has relied primarily on lower oil consumption and inventory draws to balance, although increased oil production outside Executive Summary the Middle East has also contributed. Global observed oil inventories were drawn down at an average rate of about 2.4 million barrels a day (mb/d) from March to September, helping to buffer a persistent production deficit (figure 1.B). Global oil consumption has nonetheless proved responsive to higher prices, declining by 5 mb/d (y/y) in 2026Q2 and 3.7 mb/d in Q3.

Several producers outside the Gulf have ramped up output, collectively adding nearly 2.2 mb/d, on average, since the conflict began, while trading patterns have adjusted to connect importers usually dependent on the Gulf with alternative suppliers. In 2026Q2, during the deepest supply shortfalls in the Middle East, shifts in oil trade in the United States and China illustrated these trends. U.S. exports of crude oil and oil products increased by about 1.7 mb/d relative to February, enabled by inventory releases and a pickup in production, while China’s imports declined by more than 5 mb/d as refinery runs fell and oil stocks were drawn (figure 1.C). The global oil production surplus last year, which exceeded 2 mb/d in 2025Q4, also reduced the extent of the adjustments to global demand (figure 1.D).

The Middle East conflict has dealt a historic shock to energy supplies, but several other shocks are also hitting commodity markets. Hostilities between Russia and Ukraine are impeding Black Sea grain and oilseed shipments and constraining Russia’s output of oil products, notably diesel. A very strong El Niño threatens the production of agricultural commodities. In addition, supply constraints amid demand from renewables- and technology-linked investment have propelled base metals prices higher. Overall, commodity prices are projected to increase by 23 percent in 2026, to their second-highest level since 2013, led by a 32 percent jump in energy prices. As global oil production drops more than 5 percent in 2026, Brent oil prices are forecast to remain elevated in the near term, averaging $91 per barrel for the year.

Oil prices would be higher still if oil demand were not set to fall 2.5 percent this year, the third-largest drop behind the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and the oil crisis in 1980. Food commodity prices are on track to climb by 10 percent in 2026, well above the April forecast. Metal and minerals prices are projected to reach an all-time high. In 2027, commodity prices are forecast to decline by 7 percent, with Brent prices receding to $79 per barrel and slight reductions in other energy and metal prices, but a further 7 percent rise in food prices. Even so, 2027 price projections have mostly been revised up since April, by 14 percent for energy. The forecast hinges on a confluence of moderating factors: no major escalation of the Middle East conflict, a recovery in Russia’s oil output, easing constraints on Black Sea food shipments, and manageable crop losses from El Niño.

Setbacks on these fronts could mean persistently high energy prices and stress in food markets. In an adverse scenario, oil prices would average $105 per barrel in 2027, and food prices would exceed their 2022 level. Such developments would drive global inflation higher and worsen food insecurity.

Global oil market balance, 2022Q1–2026Q2 Russia and the Middle East dropped by an estimated 60 percent (y/y) in September, with about half the shortfall offset by other exporters. Global constraints on refining capacity have therefore pushed refining spreads beyond historical norms, even during crude oil price surges (figure 2.B). Steep increases in the cost of diesel contributed to International Energy Agency (IEA) member countries agreeing in early October to release 100 million barrels of oil reserves through January 2027, initially focused on diesel. Diesel prices dipped with the announcement, but the decline reversed in subsequent weeks. As the Middle East conflict has extended, and with the Northern Hemisphere winter coming into view, upward pressure has mounted on natural gas prices in economies dependent on liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports.

By mid-October, European natural gas prices, which are largely determined by spot LNG prices, had nearly tripled from preconflict levels. Although LNG transits through the Strait of Hormuz have recently started to increase, far fewer LNG vessels than crude tankers have transited since the June memorandum of understanding between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States did not produce a follow-on agreement. Even with improved flows in September, LNG shipments were estimated at only about one quarter of pre-conflict cargoes. The expansion of LNG supplies from elsewhere is fundamentally constrained by infrastructure requirements to liquefy and transport gas. Agricultural markets are experiencing a confluence of shocks.

A very strong El Niño has begun to influence production and prices in markets including rice and sugar, while producers are bracing for pockets of flooding, drought, and heat stress across multiple regions (figure 2.C; box 1). The prospect of powerful weather shocks adds to the challenge of navigating elevated input costs for fuel and some fertilizers—although urea prices declined in 2026Q3, diammonium phosphate prices continued to rise. Food prices would likely have risen even more in recent months if not for near-record supplies of staple grains coming out of the global 2025–26 season. The World Bank Group’s metals and minerals index (which excludes precious metals) has increased by 31 percent this year, relative to the first nine months of 2025. Since April, prices of aluminum, copper, and tin have all hit records. Copper mine output has been somewhat lower than anticipated, while aluminum prices were driven to new peaks in May by conflict-related declines in supply from the Middle East. Meanwhile, the prospect of additional U.S. tariffs has increased inventory demand for copper.

More broadly, structural conditions for a sustained spell of elevated base metal prices appear to be in place as global investment transitions toward more base-metal-intensive sectors and supply growth remains relatively limited. For precious metals, pronounced geopolitical and policy uncertainty continues to sustain high prices, amid marked volatility (figure 2.D). Gold, silver, and platinum prices regained upward momentum starting in July, lifting average January to September prices for 2026 by 42, 71, and 110 percent, respectively. Beyond the drivers of individual commodity prices, commodity market connectedness— defined as the extent to which the volatility of one commodity price can be explained by shocks to other commodity prices—has shifted over time (special focus; figure 3.A).

Variation in connectedness can reflect global shocks that trigger common commodity price reactions, or idiosyncratic shocks that induce changes via substitution or complementarity relationships, or supply chain connections. Linkages that transmit price volatility from one commodity to others (transmitted connectedness) tend to become more pronounced when economic or commodity market stress episodes arise, including following the start of the current Middle East conflict (figure 3.B). On average, industrial metals transmit the most volatility to other commodity groups, likely because they are a bellwether for broader economic cycles (figure 3.C). At the onset of the Middle East conflict the primary transmitters of price volatility were oil and aluminum, both subject to direct supply disruptions, while precious metals also played a prominent role amid geopolitical strains (figure 3.D).

Rise in transmitted connectedness after the Middle East conflict started Outlook The baseline commodity price forecast assumes no major intensification of hostilities in the Middle East. In addition, it is assumed that Russia’s capacity to export oil returns broadly to normal next year, with attacks affecting Black Sea shipping also easing. The likely impacts of El Niño on agricultural commodities are assessed with reference to past very strong episodes. Global economic growth is assumed to remain moderate, in line with the recent consensus among private sector forecasters, while investment in sectors like data centers and renewables—important drivers of metal demand—is expected to remain robust.

On this basis, the World Bank Group’s commodity price index is forecast to increase by 23 percent in 2026 (y/y), reaching its second-highest level since 2013, before prices retreat by 7 percent in 2027 (figure 4.A; table 1).1 Energy In the baseline, energy prices are set to increase by 32 percent (y/y) this year, then retreat by 12 percent in 2027. Relative to the April forecasts, projected energy prices have been revised higher by 7 percent for 2026 and 14 percent for 2027, reflecting longer but less intense Middle East supply disruptions. The Brent oil price is projected to average almost $100/bbl in 2026Q4, as the global oil market remains in deficit amid tanker shortages and continued attacks on vessels, resulting in an average price of $91/bbl for the year.

Although month-to-month volatility in export flows may continue, the recent increase in crude shipments from the Gulf is assumed to prove durable overall, allowing global oil production to near its 2025 level in 2027. Rising crude supplies are expected to ease market tightness, supporting a decline in prices to an average of $79/bbl next year. Global oil consumption is anticipated to contract by 2.6 mb/d (2.5 percent) in 2026, the third- largest decline on record, after the pandemic year of 2020 and the oil market turmoil of 1980.

Consumption is expected to rebound by about 2 percent next year as oil-intensive activity recovers, but behavioral and policy-induced shifts away from oil are likely to leave a lasting imprint, reducing the oil intensity of economic activity. In 2027, after multiple large shocks this decade, global oil consumption is expected to lag its 2010–19 trajectory by more than 9 percent, roughly double the comparable anticipated shortfall in global economic output (figure 4.B).

Global oil supply is projected to fall by 5.5 mb/d (5.2 percent) in 2026, the largest decline in more than four decades outside the 2020 global recession. Modest increases in oil output in advanced economies, such as Canada and the United States, as well as in Latin America and the Caribbean, are on track to offset only a small share of very large production losses in the Middle East (figure 4.C). Next year, operational adaptations that have facilitated increased crude oil exports from the Gulf region in recent months are assumed to remain effective, allowing shipments to continue gradually building. A recovery in the global production of refined products is likely to lag. Refinery throughput is anticipated to recover to preconflict levels around mid−2027, as repairs to refineries and export facilities progress in the Middle East and Russia, and refining capacity expands elsewhere.

On this basis, absent additional lasting damage to oil infrastructure, global oil production is projected at about 106 mb/d in 2027, returning the market to a substantial surplus in the second quarter. European natural gas prices, after surging by a projected 58 percent (y/y) this year to $19 per million British thermal units ($/mmbtu), are expected to fall by only 8 percent next year to $17.5/mmbtu—a large upward revision from the April forecast. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY COMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 6 Beverage prices are expected to retreat by 24 percent (y/y) in 2026, as both cocoa and coffee production recover from past disease- and weather-related declines. Average beverage prices are forecast to broadly stabilize thereafter, as declining coffee prices partly offset a pickup in cocoa prices. In all, the World Bank Group’s agricultural commodity price index—a composite measure for food, beverages, and raw materials—is forecast to inch up this year, then gain 5 percent in 2027. The effects of El Niño are evident in several price forecast revisions relative to April 2026. The palm oil price forecast, for instance, has been revised higher by 15 percent in 2027 amid unusually dry conditions in Indonesia.

Adverse weather conditions related to El Niño have also disrupted the planting and harvesting of rice and sugar, for which 2027 price forecasts have been revised up by 21 percent and 12 percent, respectively. Next year’s projected average cocoa price, while still well below the 2025 level, has also been raised by nearly 30 percent since April. Despite substantial challenges for a subset of commodities, the overall impact of El Niño on food commodity prices is expected to be manageable, consistent with historical experience (figure 4.D). At the global level, price pressures are likely to be mitigated by the varied nature of the related weather effects, which can lift production in some locations while hindering it in others. Solid harvests in aggregate for key crops are also likely to help contain price increases.

For example, although global grain output is anticipated to drop somewhat this year, total grain supplies in 2026– 27 are still expected to be 3 percent larger than in 2024–25. Moderate effects at the global level, however, do not preclude El Niño-driven price spikes in specific locations. Average fertilizer prices are anticipated to rise by 14 percent (y/y) in 2026, mainly reflecting a surge in urea prices earlier in the year, which has since subsided owing to accelerated exports from China, among other factors (figure 4.E). Some other fertilizers, including potash, are nonetheless set for sets marginal natural gas prices in many European and Asian economies.

LNG production is more concentrated in economies heavily affected by the conflict than oil production, and natural gas output in the Middle East is expected to remain below its 2025 level in 2027, in large part because of damage to LNG trains in Qatar. Although natural gas production is projected to expand elsewhere next year, global demand is also anticipated to recover, such that Asian and European markets remain notably tight. Meanwhile, U.S. natural gas prices are forecast to increase by 6 percent in 2027 from much lower levels, partly owing to increasing LNG export demand. Coal prices are on course to climb by 25 percent (y/y) in 2026 on stronger demand and supply constraints. Prices are then projected to ease by 4 percent next year, as demand for coal as a substitute fuel softens amid lower energy prices more broadly and the expansion of renewables.

Global coal consumption is expected to inch down next year, driven mostly by declines in Europe, with coal output edging higher owing to increased production in China and India. Agriculture and fertilizers Average food commodity prices are expected to rise by 10 percent (y/y) in 2026. This partly reflects the early effects of El Niño on actual and prospective supplies of tropical commodities. However, larger impacts stem from the knock-on effects of high energy prices and from disruption to food commodity exports through the Black Sea owing to attacks on maritime infrastructure. In 2027, food commodity prices are forecast to climb by another 7 percent, led by a 9 percent rise in grain prices. This mainly reflects headwinds to rice production in Asia and wheat production globally, generally related to deteriorating growing conditions, in some cases because of El Niño.

Oils and meals prices are projected to increase by 8 percent, driven by soybean-derived products because of robust demand for animal feed and biofuels, as well as El Niño-related curbs on palm oil production.

Next year, fertilizer prices are forecast to revert to about 2025 levels, premised on declining energy costs and improved access to inputs such as ammonia and sulfur. Metals and minerals The World Bank Group’s metals and minerals price index is projected to reach a new high in 2026, rising by a projected 25 percent (y/y). Prices of base metals, including aluminum, copper, and tin, are on track for large gains reflecting various supply constraints and growing investment in energy transition and other advanced technologies. Meanwhile, iron ore prices weigh on the aggregate index amid tepid traditional construction investment, especially in China.

The metals and minerals index is projected to edge 3 percent (y/y) lower in 2027 as supply conditions improve somewhat for several base metals owing to fading production or export disruptions and new capacity coming on stream. For copper, however, mined supply growth is anticipated to remain subdued, reflecting factors such as declining ore grades in Chile, the world’s largest producer. Assuming global economic growth holds up, buoyant base metal demand driven by, for example, the expansion of renewable energy infrastructure, electric vehicles, and data centers is likely to keep medium-term prices elevated (figure 4.F). Precious metal prices are also expected to register a steep average increase of 40 percent in 2026, amid strong demand for diversifying financial assets against a strained geopolitical backdrop. Gold and silver are both in line to set annual price records.

Precious metal prices are assumed to moderate somewhat in 2027 as recent increases in advanced economy interest rates soften financial investment flows into non-yielding assets, and high prices incentivize innovation to minimize industrial use. Precious metal prices are nonetheless expected to remain at more than three times their 2015–19 average. Risks Risks to the commodity price projections are tilted toward higher prices, owing to both the severity of such risks and their potential to amplify each other. The greatest risk is that intensified hostilities in the Middle East again sharply curb oil exports. Larger-than-expected conflict-related disruptions in Russia and Ukraine could also drive up commodity prices. El Niño could destabilize agricultural commodity production more than anticipated, generating another source of price increases.

On the other hand, a durable settlement of the Middle East conflict could see energy prices plunge, exerting downward pressure on wider commodity prices. The broadest risk of lower- than-forecast prices is that global economic growth disappoints. Risks of higher commodity prices Renewed conflict-driven energy supply losses Although shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has recently increased, attacks on vessels have continued. A major, sustained re-escalation of hostilities in the Middle East could again constrict crude oil flows and further squeeze global supplies of refined oil products and LNG. The recent attack on the East-West Pipeline highlights that bypass routes are also vulnerable to disruption.

Moreover, Gulf pipelines are assumed to be fully operational in the baseline, but damage to this infrastructure or more strikes on ships in the Red Sea could deepen a renewed oil supply shortfall. Conflict-related risks to oil markets are not limited to the Middle East. Although Russia’s exports are assumed to be unconstrained next year in the baseline, damage to its infrastructure meaningfully reduced oil product exports in 2026Q3 (figure 5.A). If outages at oil facilities in Russia continue at their recent frequency, global oil production could further undershoot projected consumption, with diesel shortages a particular concern. Any worsening of oil export prospects in the Middle East or Russia would occur against a backdrop of depleted strategic and commercial energy stocks,

An exceptional El Niño could result in weather events of extreme severity in unexpected locations, with flooding and droughts undermining growing conditions for commodities including rice, palm and coconut oil, soybeans, cocoa, and coffee. This could significantly lift prices of beverages, oils and meals, and grains. At the same time, any extension of recent strikes targeting grain shipments in the Black Sea could push maize and wheat supplies from Russia and Ukraine—collectively the source of about 30 percent of global wheat exports—below projections, raising prices.

These shocks, especially if coupled with continued high energy prices, could transform the moderate food price increases in the baseline into a period of severe food stress more akin to the early 2010s. Adverse commodity price scenario In an adverse scenario for commodity prices, several conflict- and weather-related shocks to energy and food markets coincide next year. A re-escalation of hostilities in the Middle East reduces oil supplies from the Gulf region over the first half of 2027 by about 5 mb/d, relative to the baseline. Over the same period, an extended campaign of strikes on oil infrastructure keeps Russia’s crude oil and oil product exports close to their 2026Q3 volumes. T ogether, these factors reduce global oil production to about 100 mb/d in the first half of next year. Subsequently, the disruptions gradually abate, with conditions reverting toward those in the baseline.

These events generate further rapid depletion of oil stocks early next year, increasing concerns about inventories becoming scarce. Under these circumstances, the Brent oil price averages $105/ bbl in 2027, an increase of 15 percent from 2026, and 33 percent above the 2027 baseline (figure 5.B). Wider energy prices would also materially exceed forecasts, given lower LNG supplies and stronger demand for coal as an alternative fuel. heightening the sensitivity of markets to further challenges. This could be amplified by continued conflict-related weakness in Russia’s oil exports, including refined products such as diesel. Risks of lower commodity prices A durable resolution of the Middle East conflict A durable settlement of the conflict in the Middle East could alleviate threats to shipping in the region, facilitating an accelerated release of pent-up crude stocks through the Strait of Hormuz and other channels. Prices would then decline rapidly as supplies ramp up and concerns about declining inventories and future disruptions abate. The recovery of oil product supplies would likely still be somewhat delayed, although if physical risks were drastically reduced, some refinery repairs might also be expedited. Weaker-than-expected global economic growth The baseline forecast assumes that global economic growth remains resilient over the forecast horizon. If global growth were to instead slow meaningfully, and for reasons other than commodity-driven shocks, then weaker demand generally would result in lower-than-forecast commodity prices. These effects would likely be pronounced among commodities with heightened exposure to cyclical sectors, notably energy and metals, as well as some raw materials such as rubber (figure 5.D).

A drop in base metal prices could be especially pronounced if growth slowed in part because of a dimming of prospective returns from investment in artificial intelligence, with an attendant sharp tightening of global financial conditions that would hamper broader capital spending. Broader implications The expected trajectory of commodity prices in the baseline forecast and the risks associated with that forecast have broader potential consequences for the global economy. These include implications for global inflation, monetary policy stances in advanced economies and emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs), food insecurity, and the policy challenge of confronting destabilizing commodity shocks. Inflation and interest rates Prior to the conflict in the Middle East, global inflation was expected to decline this year.

The energy shock since March has rekindled inflationary pressures, with energy directly contributing about 1 percentage point to inflation across the G7 in recent months (figure 6.A). Whether these dynamics intensify in 2027 will depend substantially on the path of energy prices. Given the baseline commodity price forecasts, energy-driven inflation would likely turn negative globally around the second quarter of next year, subtracting from headline inflation. If risks instead materialize such that energy prices and headline inflation continue to rise, higher fuel costs could affect core inflation through second-round effects or destabilize inflation expectations. Under these conditions, central banks, already facing salient public memory of the postpandemic inflation surge, may judge that a spell of tighter monetary policy is necessary.

Risks Risks to the food commodity price outlook remain tilted to the upside. El Niño’s effects on production could prove more severe than anticipated, adding to upward price pressures. Prolonged hostilities in the Black Sea could further disrupt future grain shipments, and new trade restrictions could push prices above current forecasts. Intensified supply disruptions from the Middle East conflict could raise energy prices above forecast and further boost biofuel demand.

Upside risk: Stronger-than-expected local weather impacts of El Niño Stronger-than-expected drought and heat stress in major producing regions could curtail production, particularly of rice, edible oils, and sugar, raising their prices above the forecasts (box 1). Similarly, stronger-than-expected El Niño-induced heavy rains and flooding could damage crops and disrupt

The effect on prices will depend on the location and scale of specific events arising from the interaction of El Niño with local weather conditions. It will also depend on prevailing commodity-specific inventory levels relative to consumption and the ability of consumers to substitute across commodities. Upside risk: Prolonged disruptions to Black Sea shipments The baseline price forecasts assume that disruptions to Black Sea shipments will persist through 2026Q4 but ease materially in 2027, given the potential for alternative export routes to become available and for arrangements to protect much-needed grain shipments, akin to the 2022–23 Black Sea Grain Initiative.

If attacks on ports and grain infrastructure instead continue into 2027 at their recent intensity, and adequate alternative routes are not available, exports from Russia and Ukraine, which together account for one-third of global wheat exports and half of sunflower oil exports, could face prolonged disruption. In that case, it would logistically become extremely challenging to transport the region’s large grain and oilseed harvests expected in 2026–27, and grain prices could substantially exceed the forecasts (figure 14.A). Upside risk: Export restrictions Given the heightened extreme weather risks linked to El Niño, governments may become more inclined to introduce food export restrictions intended to insulate domestic consumers from cost pressures.

Historically, however, such measures have often tightened supplies in international markets, amplified volatility, and raised global prices further. During the 2010-11 food price spike, for example, such measures are estimated to have accounted for 40 percent of the rise in world wheat prices and one-quarter of the rise in world maize prices (figure 14.B; Ha, Kose, and Ohnsorge 2019). More recently, India’s July 2023 ban on non-basmati rice exports, in response to El Niño-related yield concerns, led to a 35 percent increase in world rice prices (Nes, Schaefer, and Yu 2025). Although El Niño-triggered trade restrictions have not been significantly imposed so far, a renewed wave of export restrictions could push food prices above forecasts, especially commodities that are thinly traded.

Upside risk: Higher-than-expected energy and fertilizer input costs The baseline commodity price forecasts imply meaningful decreases in agricultural input costs next year, in the form of lower energy and fertilizer prices (figure 14.C). Among other factors, this reflects assumptions that crude oil exports from the Middle East approach pre-conflict levels, that global LNG supplies gradually improve, and that Russia lifts its restrictions on oil product exports. If conflicts instead intensify energy supply challenges, agricultural input costs could exceed expectations, with higher production costs passed on to food prices. Should higher feedstock prices and renewed constraints on exports also push up fertilizer prices, farmers could cut application rates, thus lowering crop yields, reducing future supplies, and adding to food price pressures.

Upside risk: Higher biofuel demand Elevated crude oil prices and expanded biofuel mandates, especially in Brazil, Indonesia, and the United States, have contributed to increased biofuel production and higher prices for edible oils, sugar, and maize (figure 14.D). Further fuel and crude oil price increases relative to feedstock costs could widen biofuel margins and lift food commodity prices above projections. On the other hand, lower-than-expected fuel and crude oil prices, for instance because of a swifter-than-antic- ipated recovery in global supplies, could weaken feedstock demand and prices. Changes to blending mandates and their enforcement could also shift demand in either direction. Over the longer term, greater investment in nonfood feedstocks could reduce biofuel-linked demand for food-based feedstocks, dampening a recurrent source of price volatility.

AGRICULTURECOMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 35 El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a recurring climate phenomenon characterized by fluctuations in sea surface tempera- tures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific and the associated changes in atmospheric circulation. It brings drier-than-average conditions to Australia, Central America, the Ethiopian highlands, the Sahel, Southern Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and northern South America. Conversely, it causes above- average rainfall, and sometimes flooding, in southeast- ern South America, equatorial East Africa, and the southern United States (figure B1.1).

Episodes of El Niño vary considerably in intensity (figure B1.2.A).a Since 1950, there have been 27 El Niño episodes, four of which were very strong (in 1982–83, 1991–92, 1997–98, and 2015–16), with the current episode expected to become the fifth. Over the same period, there were 3 strong, 9 moderate, and 11 weak episodes. El Niño episodes typically emerge around May or June, strengthen through the third quarter of the year, peak near year-end, and dissipate during the first half of the following year. As a result, much of the associated rainfall anomaly occurs during the second half of the year, overlapping with the growing season for several major internationally traded commodities.

BOX 1 The 2026-27 El Niño: Implications for commodity markets El Niño, a major recurring source of global weather variability, alters rainfall and temperature patterns over a large geographical area, with consequences for commodity markets. The current episode, expected to reach very strong intensity and persist into early 2027, is likely to have a moderate effect on aggregate global food commodity price indexes, but could substantially affect individual commodities. The largest effects are likely for commodities whose exports are concentrated in highly exposed countries, such as rice, soybeans, palm oil, coffee, and cocoa, which have historically experienced some of the largest price increases following El Niño conditions. Wheat and maize exports, by contrast, originate mainly in less exposed countries, which, together with ample stocks, should limit the impact on their prices.

However, tight edible oil markets and overlapping shocks, such as prolonged disruptions in the Black Sea and the Middle East or new export restrictions, could amplify El Niño’s effects. Beyond commodities, highly exposed emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) could face heightened domestic food price inflation and increased food insecurity pressures. How El Niño affects commodity markets El Niño affects agricultural commodity markets predominantly by changing temperature and precipita- tion in major producing regions. Drought or excess rainfall reduces crop output, while flooding disrupts harvesting, storage, and transport. El Niño also affects non-agricultural commodity markets. Drought reduces hydropower generation, constrains mining operations, and disrupts shipping corridors such as the Panama Canal.

Heavy rainfall disrupts open-pit mining, road transport, and logistics, while warmer conditions raise electricity demand for cooling. These effects raise production and transport costs and propagate through supply chains. While El Niño’s reach is global, its effects can be highly localized. About two-thirds of countries in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), and half of those in East Asia and Pacific (EAP), are highly exposed to El Niño. All countries in South Asia (SAR) are either highly or moderately exposed (figure B1.2.B).b The impact of El Niño on commodity prices varies widely because its direct weather effects interact with inventories, demand conditions, crop substitution, and trade policies. Historical patterns show that agricultural commodity prices, including food, are on average higher following El Niño months than after neutral a.

An event is classified according to the highest category threshold met or exceeded for at least three consecutive overlapping three-month periods. b. FERTILIZERSCOMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 39 Recent developments Nitrogen (urea) prices averaged $399/mt in 2026Q3, down 42 percent (q/q) and 18 percent (y/y), after peaking at $857/mt in April (figure 18.A). Prices eased further in the first half of October. China’s urea exports are expected to reach 7.0 million metric tons (mmt) in 2026, up from 4.9 mmt in 2025.

Although an export ban imposed after the start of the Middle East conflict cut exports to near zero between March and June, China’s urea exports in the first eight months of 2026 matched the level of a year earlier, at about 1.4 mmt, with two-thirds shipped in July and August (figure 18.B). This ramp-up of exports helped replace a sizable portion of supplies blocked by the initial near closure of the Strait of Hormuz. It also highlights China’s potential role as a swing supplier, given its large coal-based urea industry, accumulated inventories previously under export restrictions, and capacity additions in 2026. DAP (diammonium phosphate) prices rose by 4 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q), extending the 20 percent increase in 2026Q2 to narrowly exceed their year-earlier level.

Conflict-related shortages of sulfur, a key input in the production of DAP , due to disruptions in the Middle East continued to constrain supply, although shortages began to ease in October as sulfur shipments reportedly crossed the Strait of Hormuz. Prices of ammonia, another key input of DAP , remained 8 percent higher in September than a year earlier, with 15 percent of global ammonia trade also disrupted by developments in the Strait (figure 18.C). European natural gas prices, at 91 percent higher than a year earlier in 2026Q3, have raised ammonia production costs for suppliers in Europe. China’s DAP export ban, in place since October 2025, further tightened supplies and supported prices. MOP (muriate of potash, or potassium chloride) prices eased by 5 percent in 2026Q3 (q/q) but remained 7 percent higher than a year earlier.

As a result, MOP remains the most affordable fertilizer relative to food prices (figure 18.D). A shift in global investment toward base-metal-intensive sectors is underway, together with constraints on supply expansion arising from decade-plus timelines for exploration and mine construction for some metals, and limited refining capacity for others.

Geographically concentrated processing and refining, alongside growing trade restrictions— including export curbs by major producing economies and import tariffs in major consuming economies—also leave some markets vulnerable to disruptions and supply shortages. SPECIAL FOCUS COMMODITY MARKETS OUTLOOK | OCTOBER 2026 48 Introduction Commodity prices often move in tandem because many markets are exposed to common shifts in global activity, input costs, trade, and financial conditions. For instance, a slowdown in industrial activity can weaken demand for energy and industrial metals at the same time, while disruptions to energy supply can raise transport and fertilizer costs and spill into agricultural markets. Periods of financial or geopolitical stress can broaden these movements across otherwise distinct commodity groups (World Bank 2024). Understanding these linkages is key because commodity price shocks affect inflation, fiscal revenues, trade balances, and food and energy security, particularly in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) with large commodity exposures (Balcilar, Usman and Agan 2024; World Bank 2026a).

Most commodity analysis appropriately focuses on the supply and demand fundamentals of individual markets. While that approach remains important, it provides only a partial view when volatility associated with one commodity is linked to developments in other commodity markets. This Special Focus examines price volatility connectedness across 15 internationally traded commodities in six groups—energy, food, industrial metals, livestock, precious metals, and soft commodities (such as coffee and cotton)— using daily data from 2006 to 2026. Price volatility connectedness measures how much of the variance in a commodity’s price volatility can be explained by shocks affecting prices in other commodity markets.

The methodology applies the Diebold-Yilmaz connectedness framework to estimate how much volatility is transmitted across commodities and how these relationships evolve over time (Diebold and Yilmaz 2009, 2012, 2014; Demirer et al. 2018). The analysis addresses the following questions: • How extensive is commodity price connectedness within and across commodity groups? • Which individual commodities play particularly important roles in linking otherwise distinct commodity groups? • How does commodity price connectedness change during episodes of global stress? The analysis presents four main findings: • Commodity-specific factors remain the dominant source of price volatility, although cross-market transmission is important. On average, roughly two-thirds of commodity price volatility is Special Focus Commodity Price Connections: How Does Volatility Spread?

Commodity price fluctuations are highly consequential for economic conditions in many emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). Moreover, individual commodity prices often move in tandem with other commodity prices, so determining the origin of price volatility can be challenging. Using a measure of price volatility connectedness across 15 internationally traded commodities over 2006–26, commodity-specific factors are found to dominate price volatility: roughly two-thirds is commodity-specific, while about one-third is associated with shocks in other commodity markets. About half of measured connectedness reflects links within broad commodity groups. Industrial metals and food are the principal net-transmitting groups, while livestock and soft commodities are the main net receivers.

At the individual commodity level, copper, maize, oil, and silver stand out as important bridges across groups. Connectedness rises during episodes of global stress: the global financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the recent conflict in the Middle East are all associated with increases in cross-market connectedness. These results suggest that market-specific analysis can be complemented by monitoring cross-market transmission, particularly during periods of global stress.

The products include crude oil and U.S. natural gas in the energy group; aluminum, copper, nickel, and zinc in the industrial metals group; maize, soybeans, and wheat in the food group; live cattle and lean hogs in the livestock group; gold and silver in the precious metals group; and coffee and cotton in the soft commodities group.3 The common sample spans May 5, 2006, the earliest date for which data are available, to June 26, 2026. Price volatility is measured using the range-based estimator of Garman and Klass (1980), which combines daily opening, closing, high, and low prices. T o capture relationships across a relatively large number of markets, the analysis estimates an elastic net vector autoregression model (appendix SF .1).

This approach uses regularization to obtain stable estimates, while retaining the most informative cross-market relationships (Demirer et al. 2018; Zou and Hastie 2005). The estimated model is used to calculate how much of each commodity’s future volatility is associated with shocks in its own market and with shocks in other commodity markets.

The following types of connectedness are measured: • T otal connectedness describes the average cross-market price volatility transmission across commodities or commodity groups. • Self-connectedness measures the share of price volatility of a given commodity or commodity group that is associated with shocks affecting its own price. • Directional connectedness measures the volatility transmitted from a given commodity or commodity group to the rest of the commodity system (transmitted connectedness) or the volatility received from the rest of the commodity system (received connectedness). 3 Heating oil, gasoline, and soybean oil are in the Bloomberg Commodity Index but are excluded from the analysis because their close links to crude oil and soybeans could overstate connectedness.

In addition, about half of measured connectedness reflects links among commodities in the same group. • Price volatility transmission is highly uneven across commodity groups. Industrial metals and food are the principal net transmitters, as they transmit much more volatility than they receive. Livestock and soft commodities are at the other end of the spectrum, as they receive considerably more volatility than they transmit. Energy and precious metals occupy an intermediate position as they transmit and receive broadly similar amounts of volatility. • Transmission is concentrated in a small number of individual commodity markets. Copper, maize, oil, and silver stand out as important bridges across commodity groups.

Their roles differ in persistence: silver ranks among the three largest net-transmitting commodities on almost 60 percent of trading days, maize in about half, copper in just over 40 percent, and oil the least frequently, reflecting its more episode-specific importance. • Connectedness rises, and the transmission network changes, during episodes of global stress. The global financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the recent conflict in the Middle East are all associated with increases in cross-market connectedness, although the commodity groups driving the transmission differ across episodes. This points to a commodity network whose transmission of price volatility intensifies and reconfigures, instead of a single permanent transmission hub.

Taken together, these findings suggest that analysis of individual commodity-market fundamentals can be usefully complemented by monitoring cross-market transmission, especially during periods of global stress. Directional connectedness, by commodity group The variance decomposition framework is useful for describing dynamic interdependence, but it does not by itself identify structural shocks.4 Extent of connectedness The total connectedness index provides a simple measure of how much commodity price volatility is associated with shocks in other commodity markets rather than with developments specific to the commodity itself. An index value of zero indicates entirely commodity-specific volatility, while a value of 100 indicates that volatility is entirely associated with shocks elsewhere in the commodity system. Commodity price volatility exhibits substantial connectedness, but considerably less than a fully connected system would imply.

Over the sample period, cross-market transmission accounts for about one-third of total price volatility, while roughly two-thirds remains commodity specific, with the total connectedness index generally between 25 and 40 (figure SF.1.A). There is also little evidence of a sustained increase over the past two decades despite deeper trade links, financialization, and the expansion of commodity derivatives. Much of this connectedness occurs within commodity groups. The self-connectedness index computed for the six groups indicates that at least three-quarters of each group’s price volatility is associated with shocks affecting that group (figure SF.1.B). Food and livestock are among the more self-contained groups, as they display the highest values of the self-connectedness index, while energy and precious metals are relatively integrated with the broader commodity system.

Once within-group transmission is removed, the total connectedness index nearly halves, falling from about 33 to roughly 16. This pattern is consistent with the structure of commodity markets. By contrast, transmission across commodity groups typically operates through more indirect channels, such as common input costs, transportation networks, financial market linkages, or shifts in global demand, so that cross-group connectedness tends to be weaker. However, the strength of these within-group bonds varies across commodity groups. As an example, among energy commodities, transmission between oil and U.S. natural gas is relatively limited despite substantial co- production, as reflected in the low value of the within-group connectedness index, consistent with Cunado, Gabauer and Gupta (2024) (figure SF .1.C).

The aggregate measures thus establish the extent of connectedness, but not which groups primarily transmit or absorb volatility or the different roles of commodities within a group. Transmitters and receivers Commodity groups can be similarly connected to the broader system while playing very different roles within it. Directional connectedness separates volatility transmitted to other groups from volatility received from them. The full-sample results show a clear hierarchy: industrial metals and food transmit more volatility than they receive; livestock and soft commodities receive more than they transmit; and energy and precious metals are broadly balanced between the two roles (figure SF .1.D). Net connectedness—the difference between transmitted and received connectedness—provides the clearest summary of this hierarchy.

Industrial metals and food have net connectedness indexes of about 11 and 7, respectively, and their transmitted connectedness is roughly 64 to 75 percent greater than their received connectedness. Livestock and soft commodities have net indexes of approximately −4 and −8 and transmit only about half as much volatility as they receive. Industrial metals and food occupy the same end of the ranking for different reasons, and the distinction matters for how their roles should be interpreted. Industrial metals’ transmitting role may partly reflect the structure of their markets. Deep, globally integrated trading facilitates rapid price adjustment, potentially supporting transmission across commodity markets beyond direct production-chain linkages (Tiwari et al. 2022). Food commodities transmit volatility through a different mechanism.

Crops compete for the same land, water, fertilizer, and transport capacity and are linked to one another through feed demand and biofuel margins. A disturbance to one crop can consequently propagate to the others through the reallocation of acreage and inputs, and beyond agriculture through fuel and feed markets. T ransmission in this case may operate closer to a resource-constraint channel, which helps explain why two groups with little in common in terms of fundamentals both register as principal net transmitters (Karkowska and Urjasz 2024). Livestock and soft commodities are at the other end of the spectrum, with more of their volatility associated with shocks arriving from elsewhere than with volatility transmitted outward.

Energy and precious metals occupy an intermediate position: both have substantial transmitted and received connectedness, making them important conduits even though their full-sample net positions are comparatively small. These broad roles are persistent, although their intensity changes markedly across stress episodes. This hierarchy highlights why the origin and path of a commodity price shock are important. A disturbance entering through a net-transmitting group may be associated with broader subsequent volatility than a similar disturbance affecting a more insulated part of the system. At the same time, group-level measures do not reveal whether transmission is broadly shared among constituent markets or concentrated in a few individual commodities. Even relatively self-contained groups, such as livestock and soft commodities, become more integrated during periods of global stress. Net connectedness reveals persistent roles but also shifts between transmission and absorption (figures SF .3.E and SF .3.F). Industrial metals remain net transmitters in every stress episode, while food became a net receiver during COVID-19, illustrating how an increase in outward transmission can coexist with a net receiving position. Energy and precious metals are net transmitters during COVID-19 but net receivers in the other episodes.

These role reversals during COVID-19 occurred as transport demand collapsed and global portfolios rebalanced. Livestock and soft commodities remain net receivers during all stress episodes, with livestock’s net absorption increasing particularly sharply during COVID-19. Differences in the economic setting may help explain how connectedness varies across periods of global stress. Global demand disturbances tend to increase the prominence of industrial metals and energy, whose prices respond closely to cyclical conditions. Supply disruptions and geopolitical shocks can strengthen connectedness in markets most directly exposed to these shocks, while portfolio reallocation can increase the prominence of precious metals. Industrial metals’ persistent transmitting role is consistent with their close connection to global economic activity.

Metal consumption responds strongly to industrial production, as demand shocks tend to be more important drivers of metal prices than supply shocks (Stuermer 2018; World Bank 2021). For this reason, major movements in metal prices can provide insights about the state of the global economy, especially during periods of heightened economic volatility (Matsumoto, Pescatori and Wang 2023). As metal markets reflect changes in demand extending beyond the consumption of metals, their prices can provide information about the broader economy and stress. Pivotality in the commodity system is therefore not a single attribute: it reflects either a standing position between two groups or an episodic increase in the importance of channels that are otherwise latent.

Connectedness during episodes of global stress Connectedness varies over time, rising during major global stress episodes and receding as pressures ease and commodity-specific fundamentals regain importance. The total connectedness index averages about 43 during the global financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the recent Middle East conflict, compared with 32 outside of these events.5 During global stress episodes, common shocks—including those related to global activity, financial conditions, risk appetite, and transport costs—account for more commodity price volatility. As pressures ease, inventories, harvests, local supply conditions, and other commodity-specific fundamentals reassert themselves and connectedness recedes.

Greater connectedness during global stress reflects both stronger commodity-market linkages and shifts among transmitting and receiving groups. T ransmission rises across groups, led by industrial metals, especially during COVID-19 and the Middle East conflict (figures SF .3.A and SF .3.B). Food transmission remains consistently high but shows fewer stress-related spikes, while transmission from energy and precious metals rose particularly sharply during COVID-19. Livestock and soft commodities remain marginal despite higher transmission during stress. Global stress also broadens exposure to external volatility, with received connectedness above non-stress levels for every group (figures SF .3.C and SF .3.D).

Conclusion and policy implications Commodity prices are connected but far from fully integrated. Over the past two decades, about one-third of price volatility has been associated with shocks in other commodity markets, while roughly two-thirds remained commodity specific. Moreover, about half of measured connectedness reflects links within broad commodity groups, underscoring the continuing importance of market- and sector-specific fundamentals. The direction of transmission is highly uneven.

Industrial metals and food are the principal net-transmitting groups, whereas livestock and soft commodities are predominantly net receivers. Energy and precious metals are more balanced conduits. At the individual-market level, copper, maize, oil, and silver stand out as important bridges across commodity groups, although the persistence and timing of their roles differ. Connectedness also intensifies and reconfigures during episodes of global stress. The recent Middle East conflict illustrates this: disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz raised transmitted connectedness most for aluminum, oil, gold, silver, and wheat, reflecting both a physical channel operating through energy and fertilizer costs and a financial channel operating through portfolio shifts toward safe-haven assets.

Broad shocks raise cross-market transmission during periods of stress, but the groups and commodities that become most important vary with the nature of the episode. The commodity system therefore has a recognizable underlying structure without a single permanent hub. The structure of that system is best understood in terms of how shocks travel rather than where they originate. Some markets appear to transmit because they price global conditions early and are read as signals; others because they share physical inputs and constraints with neighboring markets; and a small number bridge otherwise distinct groups either continuously, by virtue of serving two sets of end-users, or episodically, when latent channels become binding.

Distinguishing among these mechanisms can help in assessing which disturbances are likely to remain contained and which are likely to be associated with broader cross-market adjustment. These findings suggest that policymakers in EMDEs should continue to undertake detailed analysis of supply, demand, inventories, trade, logistics, and policy conditions in individual markets, but this analysis can be complemented by close monitoring of cross-market transmission, particularly during episodes of stress. This perspective may be especially relevant for EMDEs that are highly exposed to commodity prices through inflation, fiscal revenues, external balances, or food and energy security.
